where: Section 2, first lines ('For a 4×4 image in 4 qubits, a 2-qubit U acts like a 2×2 filter')
problem: This contradicts Section 1. In amplitude encoding the 4 qubits store the 16-value index, so no qubit belongs to one pixel or one spatial position. A 2-qubit gate therefore mixes index amplitudes; it does not slide over 2×2 pixel windows. A student will wrongly infer that qubit pairs are image patches, and that a 4×4 image in 4 qubits somehow has 16 spatial positions to filter.
fix: Say plainly: in amplitude encoding a small gate acts on the index qubits, so the 'filter' is a fixed 2-qubit unitary reused on chosen qubit pairs; the window analogy to a classical 2×2 filter only holds when qubits map to pixels, as in angle encoding with 16 qubits.

where: Section 2 ('The reduced state can be mixed, so repeat the circuit to get counts')
problem: The 'so' gives the wrong reason. A mixed reduced state is still a fixed state; you repeat the circuit because a finite number of shots only estimates the outcome probabilities, whether the state is pure or mixed.
fix: Write: the reduced state can be mixed, and a single run gives one outcome, so repeat the circuit many times (shots) to estimate the outcome probabilities.

where: Section 3, Status sentence (also echoed in Beyond and Q6)
problem: The double negative 'no advantage on a task classical deep learning does not already solve' is easy to misread, and read literally it says the opposite of the intended point.
fix: Write: so far no experiment has shown a speed or accuracy advantage over classical deep learning on any task tried.
